article.title: EXL3: How ExLlama's Trellis Quantization Shrinks Large Language Models

blocks.text: Running a 70-billion-parameter language model on a single graphics card sounds impossible. A model that size needs roughly 140 gigabytes of memory in its native 16-bit format, far beyond the 24 gigabytes a consumer GPU offers.

EXL3, a quantization format developed by the creator of the ExLlama inference engine, compresses those weights to as few as 1.6 bits each. That compression fits a 70-billion-parameter model into under 16 gigabytes of video memory while producing text that remains coherent.

The format arrives from an unlikely path: a solo developer who built a faster way to run LLaMA models on gaming GPUs, and then kept refining the compression until it rivaled techniques from academic researchers.
The ExLlama Project

In 2023, Meta released the original LLaMA models, and a community of developers immediately began building tools to run them on consumer hardware. turboderp, a developer who uses only that handle, created ExLlama as "a standalone Python/C++/CUDA implementation of Llama for use with 4-bit GPTQ weights, designed to be fast and memory-efficient on modern GPUs". The project targeted NVIDIA's RTX 30-series and 40-series cards, achieving 173 tokens per second on a LLaMA 7B model with an RTX 4090.

ExLlama filled a gap. The existing GPTQ implementations were functional but not optimized for speed. AutoGPTQ and GPTQ-for-LLaMa worked on older GPUs, but ExLlama's custom CUDA kernels squeezed better performance from newer hardware. The project attracted a community quickly. oobabooga, creator of the widely used text-generation-webui, integrated ExLlama as a backend and published detailed benchmarks comparing quantization formats.

On August 12, 2023, turboderp announced a "preliminary, initial and tentative release of ExLlamaV2" in the original ExLlama repository. The second version was not just a faster inference engine. It introduced a new quantization format called EXL2.
EXL2: Mixed-Precision Quantization

GPTQ, the quantization method ExLlama originally supported, compresses model weights to 4-bit integers. It works well, but 4-bit is a fixed target. Every weight in every layer gets the same treatment, regardless of how important that weight is to the model's output.

EXL2 changed that. The format supports 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8-bit quantization, and it can mix those bit-depths within a single model and even within a single layer. More important weights get more bits. Less important ones get fewer. The result is a model that can target any average bitrate between 2 and 8 bits per weight, such as 3.5 or 4.65 bpw.

The selection process is automatic. ExLlamaV2 quantizes each weight matrix multiple times using different settings. It measures the quantization error for each configuration against calibration data. Then it selects a combination that minimizes the maximum error across the entire model while hitting the requested average bitrate. An independent benchmark by oobabooga on an RTX 3090 showed EXL2 at 4.9 bpw achieving a perplexity of 4.31 on Llama-2-13B, with model size of 7.86 GB and generation speed of 52 tokens per second.

EXL2 made large models practical on consumer hardware. turboderp reported that Llama-2 70B could run on a single 24 GB GPU with 2.55 bits per weight, producing "coherent and mostly stable output". A 13B model could run at 2.65 bpw within 8 GB of VRAM.
The Quantization Problem Below 4 Bits

The trade-off in quantization is straightforward: fewer bits means a smaller model, faster inference, and lower quality. At 4 bits, each weight can take only 16 distinct values. At 3 bits, that drops to 8. At 2 bits, just 4.

Not all weights contribute equally to a model's output. A small subset of high-magnitude weights, called "salient" weights, have disproportionate influence. Standard quantization methods like GPTQ treat every weight with the same bit depth, which wastes bits on unimportant parameters while starving the critical ones. This problem gets worse at lower bitrates.

GPTQ addresses part of this by processing weights sequentially and adjusting remaining parameters to compensate for errors introduced at each step. But GPTQ still assigns a fixed bit depth per layer. The format cannot give extra precision to individual weights that need it most without increasing the bitrate for the entire layer.

GGUF, the format used by llama.cpp, solves this differently. It uses block-wise quantization with individual scale factors per block, and its newer "imatrix" quantizations measure the importance of each weight using calibration data to allocate bits more intelligently. turboderp himself noted that "GGUF i-quants hold up well in comparison to SOTA formats".
Getting good quality below 4 bits requires a fundamentally different approach to how weights are encoded.
QTIP and Trellis Quantization

In June 2024, researchers at Cornell University published a paper called QTIP, Quantization with Trellises and Incoherence Processing. The paper, accepted as a Spotlight at NeurIPS 2024, introduced a method that achieved state-of-the-art results in both quantization quality and inference speed.

QTIP builds on two earlier methods: QuIP and QuIP#, which pioneered the concept of "incoherence processing". The idea is to apply a mathematical transformation called the random Hadamard transform to weight matrices before quantizing them. This transform, which runs in O(n log n) time instead of the O(n squared) time required by QuIP's original random orthogonal matrices, makes the weight values approximately independent and identically distributed, following a Gaussian pattern. When weights follow a known distribution, the quantizer can be designed to match that distribution and achieve lower distortion.

The second innovation in QTIP is the use of trellis coded quantization, or TCQ. Previous state-of-the-art methods like QuIP# used vector quantization, which quantizes groups of 8 numbers at once using a codebook of precomputed values. The codebook grows exponentially with dimension. An 8-dimensional codebook works. A 16-dimensional one would be 256 times more expensive to decode.

TCQ solves this by using a stateful decoder that separates the codebook size from the effective dimension. The trellis structure allows QTIP to quantize sequences of arbitrary length while achieving distortion close to the theoretical optimum. QTIP processes 256-element vectors, compared to QuIP#'s 8-element vectors, and reduces the distortion gap between QuIP# and the optimal quantizer by over 3 times.

The throughput formula for memory-bound inference is simple: throughput equals batch size times memory bandwidth divided by model size. A smaller model reads faster from GPU memory, producing more tokens per second. The NVIDIA H100 has roughly three times the memory bandwidth of an RTX 4090, so small-batch decoding runs about three times faster on the H100 despite the consumer card having more raw compute.
EXL3: A Streamlined QTIP

EXL3 is a variant of QTIP. Like QTIP, it uses a procedural codebook and encodes high-dimensional vectors into tail-biting trellis structures. It deviates from QTIP in two ways: how tensors are regularized before quantization, and how the quantized data is packed into memory.

The quantization pipeline works in several stages. First, calibration data passes through the model to compute a Hessian matrix for each linear layer. The Hessian captures how sensitive the model's output is to changes in each weight. The Hessian is then regularized using a diagonal factor of 0.025, random sign flips, and a blockwise Hadamard transform with a block size of 128. This regularization spreads quantization error across multiple dimensions, preventing a few outlier weights from dominating the error budget.

Next, an LDL decomposition factors the Hessian, and an LDLQ sweep processes weights in reverse order, compensating for errors as they accumulate. Weights are divided into 16-by-16 tiles, matching the native input size for modern GPU Tensor Cores. For each tile, a Viterbi-style dynamic programming search finds the optimal sequence of quantized values, minimizing the distortion for that specific group of 256 weights.

At inference time, the quantized weights are decoded using a procedural codebook generated by a Linear Congruential Generator running inside GPU registers. The full codebook is never stored in video memory. It is computed on the fly, fewer than one instruction per weight, which saves memory and reduces bandwidth pressure. A Marlin-inspired GEMM kernel handles the matrix multiplication, achieving roughly memory-bound latency under optimal conditions at 4 bits per weight on an RTX 4090.
Advantages: Size and Accuracy

EXL3's primary advantage is compression at low bitrates. The format supports any target average bitrate, mixing different bit-depths across layers to hit the requested average. A user can request 3.25 bpw, 4.0 bpw, or any other value, and the quantizer allocates bits accordingly.

The perplexity results reported by turboderp show EXL3 achieving near-FP16 performance at 6 to 8 bpw and remaining competitive down to 3 bpw on Llama 3.1 and Mistral models. The format was benchmarked against GGUF i-quants on Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.1 70B, Llama 3.2 1B, and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 using the WikiText-2 test set.

At extreme compression, the results are striking. Llama-3.1-70B-EXL3 remains coherent at 1.6 bpw, according to turboderp. With the output layer quantized to 3 bpw and a 4096-token cache, inference runs in under 16 GB of VRAM. That is a 70-billion-parameter model, which would normally need 140 GB, running on a single 16 GB GPU.

At low bitrates around 2.5 bpw, ExLlamaV3 can outperform uniform quantization methods. The mixed-precision allocation gives sensitive layers more bits while spending fewer on less critical ones. An option to boost precision on attention and shared-expert layers adds only 0.05 to 0.10 bpw to the model size while producing a "disproportionately large increase in model fidelity" for mixture-of-experts architectures.

The conversion process itself is designed to be practical. AQLM, by contrast, requires approximately 720 GPU-hours on an 8xA100 server according to turboderp, costing about $850 US at current cloud rates. EXL3 conversion takes "a couple of minutes for smaller models, up to a few hours for larger ones (70B+) (on a single RTX 4090 or equivalent GPU)". The conversion computes Hessians on the fly and uses a fused Viterbi kernel, keeping the process to a single step. Multi-GPU quantization is supported, distributing the trellis encoding workload across devices.

Note: The AQLM comparison figure of 720 GPU-hours and $850 comes from the ExLlamaV3 project documentation. turboderp, the developer of ExL3, has an interest in framing the comparison favorably. The convert.md documentation was also updated in March 2026 to remove "outdated quant duration estimates," suggesting the original time claims may have been revised.
Disadvantages: Complexity and Ecosystem

The computational intensity of EXL3 quantization is real. The Viterbi trellis search is the most demanding part of the process, Enabling GPU parallelization helps, but the encoding step requires significant compute compared to simpler formats like GGUF that use block-wise scaling. For a 70B model, even "a few hours" on a single GPU is a real commitment.

The bigger disadvantages are in ecosystem support. ExLlamaV3 runs only on NVIDIA GPUs. AMD ROCm support is listed as a to-do item and has not been implemented. GGUF, by contrast, runs on NVIDIA, AMD, and Apple Silicon through CPU, Metal, and Vulkan backends.

EXL3 models are served primarily through TabbyAPI, an OpenAI-compatible server built for ExLlama. Mainstream inference engines like vLLM and SGLang do not natively support EXL3. The model library on HuggingFace contains hundreds of EXL2/EXL3 models, compared to thousands available in GGUF format. The format is NVIDIA-only, GPU-only, with no CPU fallback for mixed CPU-GPU offloading.

EXL3 also retains the original model file structure, unlike EXL2, which renamed some tensors to normalize all models into a Llama-like layout. This design choice should make it easier to add EXL3 support to other frameworks like HuggingFace Transformers and vLLM in the future. But as of mid-2026, that integration has not happened.

The accuracy picture has a wrinkle. turboderp's own documentation notes "the occasional bump around 3 bpw is repeatable and statistically significant, likely worth investigating". This means quality at 3 bits per weight may not follow the expected smooth degradation curve. A user selecting 3 bpw expecting a clean midpoint between 2 and 4 bpw might encounter an anomaly.
Where EXL3 Fits

For users with NVIDIA GPUs who want maximum compression and are willing to use ExLlamaV3 or TabbyAPI, EXL3 offers quality at low bitrates that uniform formats struggle to match. The trellis-based approach extracts more fidelity from each bit than simpler block-quant methods, particularly below 4 bpw where every bit matters more.

For users who need broad hardware support, CPU offloading, or integration with mainstream tools, GGUF remains the practical choice. Its i-quants achieve quality that turboderp himself acknowledges as competitive. The format runs everywhere and has the largest model library. It works with popular tools like Ollama and LM Studio.

The ExLlama project has traveled from a single developer's CUDA implementation to a quantization format based on peer-reviewed research from Cornell University. EXL3 applies trellis coded quantization, a technique from the signal processing literature, to the problem of compressing neural network weights.

The result is a format that can squeeze a 70-billion-parameter model into 16 GB of video memory. Whether that advantage justifies the narrower ecosystem depends on what hardware a user has and what tools they already use.
